questions.q: A 6-month-old with epidermolysis bullosa simplex develops signs of bacterial colonization on multiple wound sites. What is the most appropriate infection control strategy to minimize antibiotic resistance while reducing bacterial burden?
opts: Initiate oral cephalosporin therapy immediately to prevent systemic sepsis
Apply topical aminoglycoside ointment continuously to all affected areas
Perform routine bathing or soaking in dilute sodium hypochlorite (~0.005%) or 0.25% acetic acid baths
Use chronic topical mupirocin to all wound sites to prevent pathogenic overgrowth
questions.exp: Dilute sodium hypochlorite (bleach) baths and acetic acid soaks safely reduce bacterial colonization without inducing antimicrobial resistance, making them the first-line intervention for colonized wounds in EB. Chronic use of topical or oral antibiotics is avoided to prevent multidrug resistance; systemic antibiotics are reserved only for proven, cultured clinical infections with signs of systemic disease. This strategy preserves antibiotic efficacy for true infections.
questions.source: [Paeds Day 9] supportive care principles, EB Nurse role

questions.q: Genetic testing in a patient with xeroderma pigmentosum reveals a defect in a gene on chromosome 9q22.23. Which complementation group is this patient most likely to belong to, and what is the geographic population with the highest prevalence?
opts: XP-B; highest in Western Europe
XP-A; highest in Japan (1 in 20,000 to 1 in 80,000)
XP-Variant; highest in the United States
XP-C; highest in North Africa
questions.exp: The XPA gene is located on chromosome 9q22.23 and encodes the protein responsible for DNA damage verification in nucleotide excision repair. XP-A is the most common subtype in Japan, accounting for approximately 90% of Japanese cases due to a founder mutation, with an incidence of 1 in 20,000 to 1 in 80,000—far higher than the USA incidence of 1 in 250,000. This geographic clustering reflects the presence of a specific founder mutation circulating in the Japanese population.
questions.memory_palace: 🏰 Palace: Japan's XP-A FORTRESS on chromosome 9 (nine samurai gates) houses 90% of Japanese cases—imagine a FOUNDER'S SHRINE where one ancient mutant samurai spawned an entire army of XP-A warriors across the island nation, making it 100× more common than in America's melting pot.

questions.q: A 6-year-old girl with a history of atopy presents with fissured, glazed erythema on the forefoot and toe pads bilaterally after wearing plastic water shoes at the pool for the summer. The condition spares the interdigital spaces and arch. Which combination of factors is MOST responsible for the pathogenesis of juvenile plantar dermatosis in this case?
opts: Autoimmune attack on basement membrane proteins triggered by chlorine exposure
Humid maceration alternating with rapid drying, friction, hyperhidrosis, and occlusive footwear compromising epidermal barrier
Dermatophyte colonization of eccrine sweat ducts with secondary immune response
Genetic deficiency in filaggrin with primary loss of cornified envelope formation
questions.exp: JPD is fundamentally an irritant contact and frictional dermatitis caused by a compromised epidermal barrier. The pathogenesis involves the physical transition from a humid, macerated environment to rapid drying, exacerbated by hyperhidrosis, occlusive/synthetic footwear, and friction from surfaces such as pool decks. This is NOT an autoimmune, genetic, or infectious condition.
questions.palace: 🏰 Palace: Imagine a castle courtyard that alternates between a WET SWAMP and a BAKING DESERT—the STONE WALLS (stratum corneum) crumble from the wet-dry abuse, with SWEATY KNIGHTS (hyperhidrosis) and STIFF PLASTIC ARMOR (occluded shoes) grinding away at the mortar!

questions.q: A 22-year-old woman presents with a solitary, sharply circumscribed, jet-black macule measuring 5 mm on her right thigh. Dermoscopy reveals a diffuse blue-black structureless center surrounded by symmetric radiating pigmented streaks. Which of the following best describes the histopathological layer predominantly affected in this lesion?
opts: Confined to the dermal-epidermal junction and superficial papillary dermis, sparing the deep reticular dermis
Extends deeply into the reticular dermis with fascicular and plexiform patterns
Restricted exclusively to the epidermis without any dermal involvement
Predominantly involves the subcutaneous fat with minimal epidermal participation
questions.exp: Reed nevus is a predominantly junctional melanocytic proliferation strictly confined to the dermal-epidermal junction and superficial papillary dermis, with spindle-shaped melanocytes characteristically sparing the deep reticular dermis. This architectural limitation is a key diagnostic feature distinguishing it from plexiform variants and deeper dermal lesions. 🏰 Palace: Imagine a REED (narrow reed) growing ONLY at the BORDER of a shallow swamp (dermo-epidermal junction), refusing to sink into the deep water (reticular dermis) below.

questions.q: A 7-year-old boy presents with symmetric, shiny erythematous patches on the weight-bearing surfaces of both feet that have progressively worsened over 2 weeks. The parents report he wears sneakers daily and sweats profusely. Notably, the toe clefts and arch areas are completely spared. Which histological finding, if present on biopsy, would be most characteristic of this condition?
opts: Acanthosis with spongiosis around the acrosyringium and eccrine sweat ducts
Subepidermal blister formation with linear IgG deposits at the basement membrane
Pseudoepitheliomatous hyperplasia with dermal fibrosis
Fungal hyphae within the stratum corneum with parakeratosis
questions.exp: Juvenile plantar dermatosis (JPD) is an irritant contact dermatitis affecting the epidermis, with the key distinguishing histological feature being inflammation specifically targeting the acrosyringium and eccrine sweat ducts. The characteristic sparing of interdigital web spaces and instep, combined with the glazed erythema on weight-bearing surfaces, is pathognomonic for JPD and helps differentiate it from tinea pedis.
questions.palace: 🏰 Palace: Picture a SWEATY KNIGHT in the castle keep, his SWEAT DUCTS (acrosyringium) leaking into the castle's WEIGHT-BEARING STONE FLOORS while his ARCHED BRIDGE TOES remain pristine—the sweat duct inflammation is the castle's architectural flaw!

questions.q: An 8-year-old girl with Kindler Syndrome who previously presented with acral blistering and photosensitivity in infancy now shows progressive poikiloderma with 'cigarette paper-like' atrophy of the dorsal hands and feet, palmoplantar hyperkeratosis, and dystrophic nails. At what level(s) does skin cleavage occur in this condition?
opts: Exclusively at the lamina lucida, similar to junctional EB
Only below the lamina densa, similar to dystrophic EB
Mixed levels: intraepidermal, through the lamina lucida, and/or sublamina densa simultaneously
Exclusively within basal keratinocytes, unique to Kindler Syndrome alone
questions.exp:
Kindler Syndrome is uniquely characterized by mixed-level skin cleavage—a distinctive feature that defines it as the fourth major category of the EB spectrum. Upon minimal trauma, ultrastructural failure can occur simultaneously at three different levels: within basal keratinocytes (intraepidermal), through the lamina lucida, and/or below the lamina densa (sublamina densa). This mixed cleavage pattern differentiates Kindler Syndrome from EB Simplex, Junctional EB, and Dystrophic EB.
🏰 Palace: Imagine a KINDLER CASTLE with THREE CRUMBLING FLOORS simultaneously—the attic (intra-keratinocyte), the main floor (lamina lucida), and the basement (sublamina densa)—all giving way at once when you sneeze on them.

questions.q: In a child with generalized severe epidermolysis bullosa with extensive denuded skin, which dressing material is most appropriate for first-line wound care and why?
opts: Traditional adhesive bandages because they provide secure fixation and bacterial barrier
Low-tack soft silicone contact layers (e.g., Mepitel, Mepilex) that can be removed without epidermal stripping
Plastic occlusive wrapping to prevent air exposure and bacterial contamination
Dry gauze packing changed frequently to allow epithelialization by secondary intention
questions.exp: Traditional adhesive bandages are absolutely contraindicated in EB as they strip the epidermis upon removal. First-line wound care uses low-tack soft silicone contact layers that provide a protective, non-adherent interface while allowing painless removal without causing additional skin loss. Other advanced options include hydrocolloids, hydrogels, and biological dressings, but silicone contact layers are preferred for their gentle handling characteristics.
questions.source: [Paeds Day 9] supportive care principles, EB Nurse role

questions.q: A 9-year-old girl with alopecia areata has a family history of the condition in her mother. Genetic testing reveals she carries HLA-DQB1*03. Which of the following best describes the significance of this HLA marker in alopecia areata?
opts: It is a marker for severe alopecia totalis or universalis exclusively
It is a general susceptibility marker for all forms of alopecia areata
It predicts resistance to JAK inhibitor therapy
It indicates absolute certainty of developing alopecia areata by age 10
questions.exp: HLA-DQB1*03 (DQ3) is a general susceptibility marker for all forms of alopecia areata. In contrast, HLA-DRB1*0401 and HLA-DQB1*0301 are specific markers associated with severe, longstanding alopecia totalis or universalis. Genetic predisposition does not guarantee disease development, and HLA typing does not predict JAK inhibitor response.
questions.source: [paeds Day 28] Alopecia areata in children + JAKi
questions.memory: 🏰 Palace: DQ3 is the GENERAL GATE guarding ALL forms of AA in the castle—DRB1*0401 and DQ7 are ELITE GUARDS for the SEVERE TOWERS of totalis/universalis only.

questions.q: A 9-year-old girl from the Indian subcontinent presents with early-onset, widespread erosive lichen planus with frequent relapses. Family history reveals similar disease in her mother and grandmother. Which HLA allele is most strongly associated with familial childhood lichen planus in this clinical scenario?
opts: HLA-A3 and HLA-B8
HLA-B27 and HLA-Aw19
HLA-Bw35 and HLA-A28
HLA-DQ2 and HLA-DQ8
questions.exp: Familial lichen planus accounts for 1.5–3.8% of cases and is characterized by early childhood onset, widespread erosive disease, and frequent relapses. The HLA alleles most strongly associated with familial LP include HLA-B27, HLA-Aw19, HLA-B18, and HLA-Cw8, which differ from non-familial associations (HLA-A3, A5, A28, B8, B16, Bw35).
questions.memory: 🏰 Palace: B27 and Aw19 are the FAMILY CREST emblems hanging in the ancestral FAMILIAL wing of the castle—when multiple relatives show erosions and relapses, these HLA flags wave above the family tomb.

questions.q: A 7-year-old boy presents with a rapidly growing, bright red pedunculated nodule on his finger that bleeds easily with minor trauma. Histopathology shows lobular proliferations of capillary endothelial cells in the superficial dermis with an epithelial collarette at the periphery. According to ISSVA classification, how should this lesion be categorized?
opts: Benign vascular tumour
Vascular malformation
Infantile haemangioma
Kaposiform haemangioendothelioma
questions.exp: Pyogenic granuloma (lobular capillary haemangioma) is officially classified by ISSVA as a benign vascular tumour, not a vascular malformation, despite its acquired and reactive nature. This classification definitively separates it from congenital vascular anomalies and reflects modern understanding of its pathobiology.

questions.q: A 2-day-old neonate with suspected epidermolysis bullosa presents to the delivery unit. Which intervention by the EB clinical nurse specialist is most critical to prevent iatrogenic skin damage during initial assessment?
opts: Immediate transfer to tertiary center for genetic confirmation before any bedside evaluation
Perform initial assessment at the birthing unit to avoid mechanical trauma from unnecessary transportation
Apply standard adhesive ECG leads and identification wrist tags for monitoring during transport
Use traditional cotton gauze dressings with pressure wrapping to stabilize fragile skin
questions.exp: Neonates with EB have extraordinarily sensitive skin vulnerable to iatrogenic stripping even with normal handling. The EB clinical nurse specialist should perform the initial assessment directly at the birthing unit, avoiding the mechanical trauma of unnecessary transportation to other facilities. Standard hospital equipment like adhesive bandages, ECG leads, and wrist tags are contraindicated as they cause blistering in fragile skin.
questions.source: [Paeds Day 9] supportive care principles, EB Nurse role

questions.q: A 5-year-old boy has 7 café-au-lait macules with smooth, 'coast of California' borders. On examination, you note axillary freckling and pigmented iris hamartomas. Genetic testing reveals an NF1 mutation. What is the key distinguishing clinical feature that differentiates his condition from Legius syndrome?
opts: Presence of multiple café-au-lait macules (≥6) in both conditions equally
Development of neurofibromas, Lisch nodules, and potential CNS tumors in NF1, which never occur in Legius syndrome
Autosomal recessive inheritance pattern in Legius syndrome versus autosomal dominant in NF1
Inguinal freckling is pathognomonic only for Legius syndrome
questions.exp: Both NF1 and Legius syndrome present with multiple café-au-lait macules and intertriginous freckling in early childhood, making clinical distinction challenging. The critical differentiator is that patients with Legius syndrome (SPRED1 mutations) never develop neurofibromas, Lisch nodules, or CNS tumors, whereas NF1 patients (NF1 gene mutations) invariably do.
questions.palace: 🏰 Palace: In the NF1 TUMOR TOWER, neurofibromas grow like vines on LISCH NODULE chandeliers and CNS tumor tapestries. In the Legius SAFE ROOM next door, the door is LOCKED—neurofibromas, Lisch nodules, and brain tumors can NEVER enter, only freckling and calm café spots remain.

questions.q: A 7-year-old child presents with a 3-day history of discrete, light pink macules and papules beginning on the face and spreading caudally. There is notable tender suboccipital, postauricular, and cervical lymphadenopathy that preceded the rash by 5 days. Which of the following best distinguishes this presentation from measles?
opts: The rash is fainter, does not coalesce extensively, and fades rapidly within 3 days
The rash presents with Koplik spots on the buccal mucosa
The lymphadenopathy is generalized rather than regional
The exanthem begins on the trunk rather than the face
questions.exp: Rubella presents with a characteristically fainter rash that does not coalesce as extensively as measles and fades rapidly (often within 3 days) in the same order it appeared. The early tender suboccipital, postauricular, and cervical lymphadenopathy preceding the rash by up to 7 days is also pathognomonic for rubella. Measles, by contrast, produces Koplik spots and a more confluent, darker exanthem.

questions.q: A 5-year-old girl with Klippel-Trenaunay syndrome presents with a port-wine stain and progressive left lower-limb hypertrophy. According to the diagnostic criteria, which of the following is MANDATORY to establish the diagnosis and differentiate it from Parkes-Weber syndrome?
opts: Presence of all three features (capillary stain, venous malformation, overgrowth) without exception
Demonstration of high-flow arteriovenous fistulae on Doppler ultrasound
Complete ABSENCE of fast-flow arterial shunts or arteriovenous malformations
Confirmed germline PIK3CA mutation on genetic testing of peripheral blood
questions.exp: The critical distinction between KTS (slow-flow combined malformation) and Parkes-Weber syndrome (fast-flow with arteriovenous fistulae) is the complete ABSENCE of arterial shunts in KTS. This is a mandatory diagnostic criterion. KTS requires only TWO of the three classic features for diagnosis, and the mutation is postzygotic/somatic (not germline), making blood genetic testing unreliable.
questions.memory: 🏰 Palace: Imagine TWO KNIGHTS entering the KTS castle—one with a PORT-WINE STAIN shield and one with VEIN OVERGROWTH armor. They DON'T need the THIRD KNIGHT (overgrowth). But at the gate stands the ARTERIAL GUARD: if she lets ANY FAST-FLOW ARTERIAL ARROWS through, you're BANISHED to PARKES-WEBER prison!

questions.q: A 3-year-old boy presents with a geographic port-wine stain on his left lower limb, progressive limb hypertrophy, and imaging reveals abnormal persistent embryonic veins with lymphatic malformations but NO arteriovenous fistulae. Which genetic mechanism BEST explains this presentation?
opts: Germline heterozygous RASA1 mutation causing familial multiple cavernous hemangiomas
Postzygotic somatic gain-of-function PIK3CA mutation activating the PI3K/AKT/mTOR pathway
High-flow arteriovenous malformations secondary to NOTCH1 haploinsufficiency
Loss-of-function VEGFc mutations causing lymphedema-distichiasis
questions.exp: Klippel-Trenaunay syndrome is driven by postzygotic somatic gain-of-function mutations in PIK3CA (encoding p110α of PI3K), which hyperactivates the PI3K/AKT/mTOR pathway—the master regulator of growth, proliferation, and angiogenesis. This somatic mosaic mutation is restricted to the affected tissue clone and explains both the vascular dysmorphogenesis and progressive overgrowth. The absence of arteriovenous fistulae distinguishes KTS (slow-flow) from Parkes-Weber syndrome (fast-flow).
questions.memory: 🏰 Palace: In the castle throne room, the **PI3K KING** (postzygotic) sits on a MOSAIC throne (somatic clone), activating an AKT ARMY marching through only ONE HALF of the kingdom (hemilimb overgrowth)—NOT the whole kingdom like germline mutations, which would decapitate the embryo.

questions.q: A 3-year-old boy presents with painful oral ulcers on the tongue and buccal mucosa, followed by characteristic vesicles on his palms and soles during summer. Which of the following best describes the morphology and orientation of the cutaneous lesions in classic hand-foot-and-mouth disease?
opts: Round or circular vesicles randomly distributed across the skin surface
Elliptical or 'football-shaped' vesicles with long axes parallel to dermatoglyphics
Linear vesicles arranged in a dermatomal distribution
Polygonal vesicles with central hemorrhagic necrosis
questions.exp: Classic HFMD caused by Coxsackievirus A16 produces pathognomonic elliptical or 'football-shaped' vesicles on the palms and soles, with their long axes oriented parallel to the natural skin lines (dermatoglyphics). This distinctive morphology and orientation helps differentiate HFMD from other viral exanthems.
questions.palace: 🏰 Palace: Picture FOOTBALL-shaped lesions LINED UP like YARD MARKERS on the PALM FIELD, all pointing parallel to the fingerprints like goal lines.

questions.q: A 19-year-old female with a pigmented spindle cell nevus on her thigh is counseled about the epidemiology of this lesion. Which statement accurately reflects the demographic characteristics of Reed nevus?
opts: It shows a strong predilection for prepubertal children with equal gender distribution
It predominantly affects young adults in their second to third decade with a 2:1 female-to-male predominance, favoring the thighs
It is more common in males and typically presents after the age of 40 years
It shows no specific age or gender predilection and occurs equally across all body sites
questions.exp: Reed nevus distinctly differs from classic Spitz nevus by showing strong predilection for the second to third decade of life (young adults), with a 2:1 female-to-male predominance and approximately 67% of lesions occurring on the extremities, particularly the thighs. This contrasts sharply with pink Spitz nevi which target prepubertal children. 🏰 Palace: Picture a YOUNG WOMAN (2:1 ratio = she brings 2 friends) standing on her THIGHS in the SECOND floor of a castle (second decade = 20s–30s), while CHILDREN play in the FIRST floor below.

questions.q: A 6-year-old boy presents with grouped erythematous papules and pinpoint pustules around the mouth, with a distinct clear zone sparing the vermillion border. The lesions lack comedones and extend to the nasolabial folds. Which of the following best describes the histopathological findings?
opts: Follicular spongiosis with perivascular and perifollicular lymphohistiocytic infiltrate
Non-caseating granulomas exclusively in the mid and upper dermis
Sebaceous gland hyperplasia with microcomedone formation
Full-thickness dermal fibrosis with minimal inflammation
questions.exp: Classic (nongranulomatous) periorificial dermatitis is characterized by follicular spongiosis and eczematous changes within the epidermis, accompanied by a perivascular and perifollicular lymphohistiocytic infiltrate (often containing plasma cells) in the superficial dermis. The absence of comedones and the distinctive 5 mm clear zone sparing the vermillion border are pathognomonic clinical features. Granulomatous changes are seen only in the rare childhood granulomatous variant (CGPD).
questions.memory_hook: 🏰 Palace: Picture a CASTLE'S SUPERFICIAL MOAT (spongiosis) filled with PURPLE LYMPHOCYTE SOLDIERS marching around the FOLLICULAR TURRETS—the classic castle's front gate (vermillion border) always remains CLEAR and UNTOUCHED by invaders.

questions.q: A 7-year-old boy presents with sudden-onset round patches of complete hair loss on his scalp. On dermoscopy, you observe hairs that are narrower at the proximal end and wider distally. Histologically, a dense peribulbar lymphocytic infiltrate is seen. Which structure is spared from the autoimmune attack in alopecia areata, allowing for potential hair regrowth?
opts: The bulge region (upper follicular stem cell reservoir)
The hair matrix cells in the lower bulb
The dermal papilla
The sebaceous gland
questions.exp: In alopecia areata, the autoimmune attack targets the peribulbar region of anagen hair follicles but spares the bulge region, which contains the follicular stem cell reservoir. This explains why alopecia areata is non-cicatricial and hair can regrow even years later. The hair matrix cells, dermal papilla, and sebaceous gland are not preserved from inflammation.
questions.source: [paeds Day 28] Alopecia areata in children + JAKi
questions.memory: 🏰 Palace: The BULGE (stem cells) sits HIGH in the castle TOWER—safe from the SWARM OF BEES buzzing below in the PERIBULB dungeon, so the kingdom's hair can rebuild from its royal reserves.

questions.q: A pregnant woman in her first trimester is exposed to rubella virus. Which genetic factor has been identified as strongly associated with increased susceptibility to rubella infection and nonresolution of disease?
opts: HLA-B27 allele
HLA-A1 allele
HLA-DR3 allele
HLA-C allele
questions.exp: The HLA-A1 allele, or genetic factors surrounding the A1 extended haplotypes, are strongly associated with increased susceptibility to rubella virus and nonresolution of the disease. This genetic predisposition is particularly clinically significant in the context of maternal susceptibility during pregnancy, as it increases the risk of fetal transmission and congenital rubella syndrome.
questions.memory: 🏰 Palace: Picture the castle's grand THRONE (HLA-A1) guarded by a RUBY RED GATE GUARDIAN (Rubella) who CANNOT REFUSE ENTRY (increased susceptibility) to the pregnant QUEEN in the castle corridor.

questions.q: A 3-year-old boy presents with severe blistering sunburns after minimal sun exposure, progressive neurological deterioration, short stature, and gonadal hypoplasia. Genetic testing confirms mutations in the XPA gene. Which of the following best describes the primary pathophysiological defect in this patient's condition?
opts: Defective DNA damage verification in the nucleotide excision repair pathway
Loss of helicase function within the TFIIH transcription-repair complex
Impaired translesion DNA synthesis across UV-induced photoproducts
Autoimmune-mediated destruction of epidermal keratinocytes with HLA-B27 association
questions.exp: Xeroderma pigmentosum group A (XP-A) results from mutations in the XPA gene, which encodes the protein responsible for DNA damage verification—the critical first step in nucleotide excision repair that detects UV-induced cyclobutane pyrimidine dimers and pyrimidine (6-4) pyrimidone photoproducts. The clinical presentation of severe sunburns, neurodegeneration, dwarfism, and gonadal hypoplasia is characteristic of De Sanctis-Cacchione Syndrome, the severe neurological variant of XP-A. XP is a genodermatosis of genomic instability, not an autoimmune condition, so HLA associations and autoimmune mechanisms are irrelevant.
questions.memory_palace: 🏰 Palace: In the grand X-ray Archives of the castle, the XPA gatekeeper stands guard at the ENTRANCE to the nucleotide excision repair ballroom—without proper damage VERIFICATION at the gate, UV photons flood through unopposed, causing catastrophic neurological collapse inside (De Sanctis-Cacchione's ghastly tower).

questions.q: A 3-year-old child presents with 8 well-circumscribed, uniformly pigmented tan-brown macules on the trunk and limbs. Histopathology shows a normal number of melanocytes in the basal layer but increased melanin production and transport into keratinocytes, with prominent giant melanosomes. What is the primary pathophysiological mechanism underlying café-au-lait macules?
opts: Autoimmune destruction of melanocytes with inflammatory cytokine cascade
Genetically driven disorder of melanin synthesis with constitutive activation of intracellular signaling pathways (Ras-MAPK or cAMP)
HLA-associated immune receptor dysfunction targeting basal layer antigens
Pathogenic antibody-mediated complement activation in the epidermis
questions.exp: Café-au-lait macules are benign, localized epidermal pigmentary anomalies caused by genetic defects driving constitutive activation of intracellular signaling cascades, not immune-mediated or autoimmune processes. The pathology strictly lacks autoimmune features, inflammatory cytokines, HLA associations, or pathogenic antibodies.
questions.palace: 🏰 Palace: Imagine a calm GENE (not angry immune cells) sitting peacefully in the basal BRICK LAYER of a tan castle, constantly OVERPRODUCING MELANIN PAINT from giant golden MELANOSOME BUCKETS—purely genetic chaos, no inflammation fighting back.

questions.q: A 10-year-old child presents with purple, polygonal, flat-topped papules on the wrists and ankles that are intensely pruritic. Histology shows a dense band-like lymphohistiocytic infiltrate at the dermo-epidermal junction with 'saw-toothed' acanthosis and Civatte bodies. Which immunological cell type is considered the primary driver of tissue damage in this child's lichen planus?
opts: CD4+ helper T-cells exclusively in the dermis
CD8+ cytotoxic T-lymphocytes directly attacking basal keratinocytes
Pathogenic IgG and IgA autoantibodies causing humoral damage
CD56+ CD16+ natural killer cells producing IL-4
questions.exp: Lichen planus is a T-cell-mediated autoimmune disorder where CD8+ cytotoxic T-lymphocytes directly attack basal keratinocytes, alongside CD4+ helper T-cells and NK cells. Direct immunofluorescence is negative for pathogenic autoantibodies (IgG/IgA), confirming cellular rather than humoral immunity as the primary mechanism.
questions.memory: 🏰 Palace: Imagine CD8 KILLERS (eight assassins) stabbing basal keratinocytes at the castle dungeon (DEJ), while IgG and IgA bouncers are turned away at the gate—only CELL-mediated weapons allowed inside.

questions.q: A 6-month-old boy presents with blistering on his hands and feet following minor trauma, along with severe photosensitivity. Genetic testing reveals loss-of-function mutations in the FERMT1 gene. Which protein is deficient in this condition, and what is its primary function?
opts: Collagen VII; anchoring fibrils below the lamina densa
Kindlin-1; linking actin filaments in basal keratinocytes to the extracellular matrix
α6β4 integrin; hemidesmosmal attachment
BP180; collagenous domain in hemidesmosomes
questions.exp:
Kindler Syndrome results from loss-of-function mutations in FERMT1 gene, leading to absence of kindlin-1, a focal adhesion protein. Kindlin-1 normally links actin filaments within basal keratinocytes to the underlying extracellular matrix, and its loss impairs keratinocyte adhesion, shape, and polarity. This structural defect distinguishes Kindler Syndrome as a genetic disorder of skin, not an autoimmune disease.
🏰 Palace: Picture a KIND GIRL (Kindlin) HOLDING HANDS (actin filaments) with the GROUND (ECM matrix) at the basement of a castle—when she lets go, the basement crumbles and blisters form.

questions.q: A 2-year-old child from Taiwan presents with initial mucocutaneous features of hand-foot-and-mouth disease, but rapidly develops brainstem encephalitis, flaccid paralysis, and pulmonary edema within days. Which enterovirus is responsible for this severe neurologic phenotype and is endemic to the Asia-Pacific region?
opts: Coxsackievirus A16
Coxsackievirus A6
Enterovirus 71
Coxsackievirus B1
questions.exp: Enterovirus 71 (EV71) is a highly virulent strain that causes severe neurologic HFMD with CNS and cardiopulmonary tropism, leading to potentially fatal brainstem encephalitis, encephalomyelitis, aseptic meningitis, and acute flaccid paralysis. Since the late 1990s, massive epidemics of EV71-associated severe HFMD have recurrently affected the Asia-Pacific region, particularly Taiwan, China, Singapore, Malaysia, Vietnam, and Australia.
questions.palace: 🏰 Palace: Picture a SKELETON'S BRAIN cracking like an egg (71 = EV-ONE-SEVEN), with the ASIAN LANDSCAPE crumbling beneath it—EV71's deadly Asian fortress.

questions.q: A 5-year-old child of African descent presents with persistent, severe periorificial eruption targeting the mid and upper dermis with prominent perifollicular involvement. Which clinical variant is most likely, and how does it differ from the classic form?
opts: Childhood granulomatous periorificial dermatitis (CGPD); occurs in prepubertal children with increased prevalence in African or Caribbean descent and granulomatous infiltration of mid-upper dermis
Classic periorificial dermatitis; occurs exclusively in women aged 16–45 years with follicular spongiosis in the superficial dermis
Perioral dermatitis secondary to topical corticosteroid overuse; primarily affects the epidermis and superficial dermis
Rosacea-like eruption triggered by fluorinated toothpaste; characterized by eczematous changes without granulomas
questions.exp: Childhood granulomatous periorificial dermatitis (CGPD) is a rare, severe variant occurring almost exclusively in prepubertal children with significantly increased prevalence in children of African or Caribbean descent. Unlike classic periorificial dermatitis (which predominantly affects women aged 16–45 and shows follicular spongiosis in the superficial dermis), CGPD is characterized by a granulomatous inflammatory response targeting the mid and upper dermis with strong perifollicular predilection. The patient's age, ethnicity, and deeper dermal involvement point to CGPD.
questions.memory_hook: 🏰 Palace: Imagine a DARK EBONY CASTLE (African descent) with DEEP STONE GRANARY CHAMBERS (mid-upper dermis granulomas) built AROUND TALL FOLLICULAR PILLARS—this fortress belongs only to YOUNG PRINCE CHILDREN, never to adult women who prefer the SHALLOW SURFACE TOWERS (superficial dermis spongiosis) of the classic castle.
